extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating prior art and making or overcoming rejections under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 (including determining public use, on-sale, printed publication/otherwise available, admissions, and application of 102(a)(1) vs 102(a)(2)). Intended for examiners preparing Office actions and practitioners responding to 102 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)) — two categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), uses of an invention before the patent's critical date that constitute a 'public use' fall into two categories: the use either '(1) was accessible to the public; or (2) was commercially exploited.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a use is a pre-AIA 102(b) public use also depends on who is making the use. A third party's use that did not obtain the invention from the inventor is invalidating only if it was accessible to the public. An inventor's own prior commercial use, albeit kept secret, may constitute a public use barring a patent. An inventor creates a public use bar when showing the invention to, or allowing use by, another person who is 'under no limitation, restriction, or obligation of confidentiality.' See MPEP § 2133.03(a) and cited cases (Woodland Trust, American Seating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)) — availability to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1), public use is limited to those uses that are available to the public — the provision has the same substantive scope with respect to uses by either the inventor or a third party as public uses under pre-AIA law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once an examiner becomes aware of a potentially public use, the examiner should require the applicant to provide information showing that the use did not make the claimed process accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: On sale — commercial sale or offer for sale (Pfaff test)
rubrics_metrics.description: On-sale activity will bar patentability if the claimed invention was: (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale, not primarily for experimental purposes; and (2) ready for patenting (Pfaff v. Wells Electronics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract law and commercial law principles apply to determine whether a commercial sale or offer for sale occurred. The enablement inquiry is not applicable to whether a claimed invention is 'on sale' under pre-AIA 102(b). See MPEP § 2133.03(b). Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) the phrase 'on sale' is treated as having the same meaning. The sale/offfer need not occur in the United States under AIA, and secret commercial activity can be an on-sale bar (see MPEP discussion and Helsinn for confidential sales).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope of on-sale (AIA vs pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), an invention was on sale only if on sale 'in this country.' Under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) there is no geographic limitation on where the sale or offer for sale may occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formulating a rejection, Office personnel should consider evidence of sales activity wherever the sale activity took place.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale can be secret or confidential (Helsinn)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pre-AIA 'on sale' provision has been interpreted as including commercial activity even if the activity is secret. The Supreme Court in Helsinn (2019) held that an inventor's sale to a third party who is obligated to keep the invention confidential can qualify as prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sale or offer for sale that does not disclose the subject matter or make the invention available to the general public may nevertheless qualify as prior art in anticipation or obviousness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Otherwise available to the public’ (AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) catch‑all)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) provides a 'catch-all' category: a claimed invention is not entitled to a patent if it was 'otherwise available to the public' before its effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision focuses on whether the disclosure was 'available to the public' rather than the means. Examples of 'otherwise available' include a student thesis in a university library, a poster at a scientific meeting, subject matter in a laid-open patent application or patent, a document electronically posted on the Internet, or a commercial transaction that does not constitute a UCC sale. Even if not a printed publication or sale, a disclosure may be prior art under this provision if the claimed invention was made sufficiently available to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement of 'by others' under AIA 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key difference between pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) and AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) is that pre-AIA required the prior art to be 'by others.' Under AIA 102(a)(1) there is no requirement that the prior art relied upon be by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, disclosures made one year or less before the effective filing date by the inventor or a joint inventor (or by another who obtained the subject matter from them) may fall within an exception under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by applicant as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions by the applicant (statements in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art') will be treated as prior art under the AIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such admissions can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102. See MPEP § 2129 and cited cases (Riverwood, Constant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'disclosure' for 102 purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA does not define 'disclosure,' and AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) does not use the term 'disclosure.' Nonetheless, the Office treats 'disclosure' as a generic expression intended to encompass the documents and activities enumerated in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) (being patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public, or being described in a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO published application).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure: Determining whether to apply 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an examiner: first consider whether the reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1); next determine if any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) apply. Separately, consider whether the reference qualifies under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and then whether any exceptions in 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents, printed publications, public use, on sale, and other availability qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) if the reference predates the effective filing date. For 102(a)(2), U.S. patents and published applications (or WIPO publications designating the U.S.) are prior art if their effectively filed date is before the claimed invention's effective filing date; the concept of 'effectively filed' is controlled by 35 U.S.C. 102(d) and MPEP § 2154. Disclosures in a potential reference within the one-year grace period may be excepted under 102(b)(1) (see MPEP §§ 2153.01, 2153.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) (one‑year grace for inventor disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure in a potential prior art reference within the one‑year grace period is excepted as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)(A) if: (1) the disclosure was made one year or less before the effective filing date; and (2) the disclosure was by the inventor or a joint inventor, or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 102(b)(1)(B) a disclosure within the one-year period is also excepted if the reference discloses subject matter that had been previously publicly disclosed by the inventor, a joint inventor, or another who obtained it from them. See MPEP §§ 2153.01(a), 2153.02 and § 717.01(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2) for 102(a)(2) references
rubrics_metrics.description: Three exception provisions limit use of patents/published applications as prior art under 102(a)(2): (A) 102(b)(2)(A) limits using an inventor's own work as prior art when it is disclosed in a patent or published application by another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor; (B) 102(b)(2)(B) excepts subject matter effectively filed by another after the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor; (C) 102(b)(2)(C) excepts subject matter disclosed in a patent/application from being prior art if, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, the subject matter and the claimed invention 'were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 102(b)(2)(C) resembles pre-AIA 103(c) (common ownership) but significant differences exist; see MPEP § 2154.02(b) for details on establishing common ownership or obligation of assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) rejection — available responses
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) can be overcome by a number of procedural and substantive paths in addition to arguing patentable distinctions or amending claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (A) Submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the 37 CFR 1.78 time period by providing the required reference to a prior application in a corrected ADS and establishing that the prior application satisfies enablement and written description requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a), or filing a grantable petition for an unintentionally delayed benefit claim. (B) Submitting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78 with required ADS corrections and establishing enablement/written description, or filing a petition for delayed acceptance. (C) Submitting a priority claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) within 37 CFR 1.55 and establishing the prior foreign application satisfies enablement/written description and is perfected by certified priority document and translation where necessary. (D) Filing an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.130: (a) attribution affidavits under 1.130(a) to except a disclosure as made by the inventor/joint inventor or by one who obtained subject matter from them; (b) prior public disclosure affidavits under 1.130(b) to except an intervening disclosure if the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor/joint inventor (or one who obtained it from them) before the intervening disclosure or before the effective filing/effective filing of the reference. (E) Establishing common ownership or evidence of a Joint Research Agreement to overcome a 102(a)(2) rejection by entitlement to the 102(b)(2)(C) exception. Note: these remedies may also be used to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2) prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs for AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections and usage rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific form paragraphs (¶ 7.06, ¶ 7.07.aia, ¶ 7.08.aia, ¶ 7.12.aia, ¶ 7.14.aia) are provided for making rejections under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and related statutory bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and examiner notes: ¶ 7.06 (Notice re prior art available under both pre-AIA and AIA) must be used in all Office Actions when a prior art rejection is made in an application with an actual filing date on or after March 16, 2013 that claims priority/benefit to an application filed before March 16, 2013; use only once per Office action. ¶ 7.07.aia (Statement of Statutory Basis) quotes 35 U.S.C. 102; statute need only be re-cited in first actions on the merits and final rejections. ¶ 7.08.aia for 102(a)(1) must be used where applicable and must be preceded by form paragraphs 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia. ¶ 7.12.aia for 102(a)(2) must be preceded by 7.03.aia and 7.07.aia and may be preceded by 7.08.aia; use only if the reference is a qualifying U.S. patent, U.S. application publication under 122(b), or WIPO publication with an earlier effectively filed date. ¶ 7.14.aia addresses pre-AIA 102(g) priority of invention language. Form paragraphs 7.07.aia, 7.08.aia, 7.12.aia and 7.14.aia are to be used ONLY ONCE in a given Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date considerations for 102(a)(2) (35 U.S.C. 102(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2), U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and international patent applications published under PCT are prior art if the effectively filed date of the disclosure is before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the issue or publication date is not before the effective filing date, the reference may qualify under 102(a)(2) if it was 'effectively filed' earlier. 35 U.S.C. 102(d) sets forth the criteria to determine when subject matter described in such documents was 'effectively filed'; see MPEP § 2154 for details.
